Media Description:
I've seen a four leaf clover. Now I also know that likelihood of a four leaf clover is 1 in 10 000, and that the Guinness world record of single stem with leafs is 63. I thought about clovers, because I was thinking about how we set expectations for testing. 

I believe we should not teach testing as easy with things everyone can find. I have been in teams where it is like that, and called those team pizza box teams. Your job as tester in a team should not be reminding that big visible items of trash of any kind should not be lying around. If it is, your 1st item of business is to have conversations that change the idea of how we deal with basics, and building a foundational culture of quality. 

So today I am suggesting that instead 'kicking tires' and finding out things with intuition that anyone with care and time could go for, testing is more like hunt of the four leaf clovers. They are there even when you don't find them. There are techniques of directing attention that make the hunt rewarding, and exploratory means you continuously learn and adapt the hunt, while tracking the coverage. 

Would people take a job as four leaf clover hunters if they never saw one? Or would they need a field that made the hunt rewarding, changing the odds? But also, if there was already a pile of recently found ones, would adding one more to the pile be rewarding to anyone?

The blockers of *time* and *shame*. Those two have real benefit stories in genAI use. People are doing things they weren't doing before, learning things they weren't able to do before. 

There are two collected experiences in particular in my mind from space of test managers: 
- doing an excel (complex one)
- creating a Jira dashboard (tailored one)

These two at first feel to me like things I learned to do 20 years ago. Granted, I took an advanced excel course to be comfortable with pivot tables and macros. And I was awarded the opportunities of configuring Jira for too many organizations over the years to learn the limits and possibilities of the tool. I was surprised the others hadn't learned those. 

Eventually, I got to the realization with a little nudging of great folks of Mastodon:
- we start our 10x from very different points, and appreciating the variety of skills and contributions in necessary
- adding shame won't help, and the best of genAI is removal of shame, allowing for time to do things we never did before but delegated or left undone. 

GenAI as learning tool is valuable.

Many of us have learned that Grace Hopper coined the advice that it is better to ask for forgiveness than permission. . Elizabeth Ayer shifted me fundamentally, when he built on Hopper and suggested *radiating intent*. 

We are, in our projects, often waiting for someone else to decide. Be it choice between Terraform and Bicep or our mutual commitment to showing a plan to a client or what day of the week we are meeting for breakfast at office, we expect "other" to contribute, and yield to a degree where things don't move forward. 

A good way of doing things that aren't quite up your alley is to radiate intent. I was inspired to think about it as I posted to my project teams that I'm picking up work that wasn't mine, needs doing, and got pushback on a necessary conversation we had first. Doing something, visibly, is a great way for taking things forward. You will notice you are rarely being blocked for a conversation when you radiate intent.

Media Description:
The workforce transformation around AI hits tester profession in an interesting way, since tester profession is one of the least homogenous masses. While the world argues on growing programming-centricity making many testers developers, there are a lot of testers I would classify as knowledge workers. Knowledge worker type of a tester stops at reporting the bug, not at fixing the bug (with growing abilities in fixing, and varying boundaries on how the work gets shared with other developers). 

I find myself tracking experiences people have already been through. 

People who are "developers" have all or most of the knowledge worker experiences too with AI. People who are knowledge workers hand off all of that developer experiences to developers. 

A lot of this split is on the tools you live with. Git-first or some WYSIWYG work support systems. For years we've believed that knowledge workers can't deal with having to see VSCode and version control, and would not recognize the computer they are on, let alone the sandbox they work on. For abstracting things away, we have designed work with a handoff. 

I have chosen to live in the developer frame. I transform people to the developer frame, and in the developer frame. But I recognize the more significant fears are in the knowledge worker frame.

A colleague in the community helped me on groundwork around ideas and expectations on what results to expect from a tester. For him to help me, I may have given an hour of teaching. I learned a lot and wanted to share some of the insights the collaboration generated. 

We were testing e-primer within capture the bugs -feedback frame . 
https://lnkd.in/dNxry3id

He proposed *positive* tests of real sentences as focus, and we learned that it is a wide concept that requires quite much imagination. Eprime is this idea of writing English voiding all forms of "to be" verb, and we came up with the You are - you're side by side. One works, one finds a bug. 

Generating the 35 essentially different classes of input is a hard problem, and it's not taught in ISTQB courses. A lot of the testing is framed as ready answers from someone else, and a lot of the testers fail at finding problems because they stick to someone else's plans. 

Added a few new features to the list of things we could consider, from tracking questions people should be asking to giving tips you can benefit from when learning but would never get with real applications.
